newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela reaches crucial social security deal.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela reaches crucial social security deal.

text.p: Venezuelan government officials and union and business leaders have reached agreement over crucial social security reforms, a union leader told Reuters.

Carlos Navarro, Secretary General of Confederation of Venezuelan Workers, Venezuela's largest union, said agreement over prestaciones, or social security payments reform, had been reached during the early hours of Saturday.
"We are just revising the final documents ... details will be announced by President Rafael Caldera on Monday," Navarro said in a brief telephone interview late Saturday.
Navarro did not outline the agreement reached in the tripartite talks, seen by many as a precondition for shrinking Venezuela's bloated bureaucracy and freeing-up labor markets.

But according to local news reports the deal includes a minimum monthly salary of between 62,000 and 90,000 bolivars ($130 - $190) to be adjusted six monthly in line with the price of a basic food basket. The current minimum salary, including bonuses, stands at around 53,000 bolivars ($110).
Leading daily El Nacional also reported Sunday that it had obtained an advanced leaked copy of the document outlining the reforms.

The social security severance system will first be brought up to date with workers paid one month's wage for each year worked, plus as bonus that has a 200,000 bolivar ($500) limit, the paper reported. Workers will receive 25 percent of that payment in cash up front, with the remaining gathering interest until it is paid over a maximum of five years.
Thereafter, under the new system, employers will place 45 days of salary into special savings accounts for the first year worked, and 60 days of salary each subsequent year.
Venezuelan business chamber Fedecamaras, which was closely involved in the discussions, said it was satisfied with the result, El Universal also reported Sunday.

"This is a conquest for a new Venezuela," the paper reported Fedecamaras president Jorge Serrano as saying. When the new system begins, it will allow Venezuelans to "progressively increase their well-being".
